issues.legal_issue: Legislation that singles out particular succession claimants, dismisses their claims, and prevents them from establishing their rights in court violates the constitutional guarantee of equal protection when the distinction has no rational basis.
material_facts: A law dismissed the succession claims of two women and their children while leaving other claimants to the estate unaffected.
The excluded claimants asserted that they were entitled to inherit under the personal law governing their community, and no competent court had determined their claims.
The legislation was intended to end a private succession dispute and relied on an adverse report by a non-judicial authority.
The dispute’s lengthy duration did not give it exceptional features warranting different treatment from other succession disputes.
issues.conclusion: The legislation was discriminatory and had no rational or reasonable basis, so it violated Article 14 and was void to the extent that it dismissed the claimants’ succession claims.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 13(2) and 14 of the Constitution, legislation must not infringe the equal-protection guarantee. A legislature may classify persons to address particular objects, and differentiation alone is not discrimination; the classification must have a rational basis related to the legislative object and must not be arbitrary. In Chiranjit Lal v. Union of India, the Court recognized the presumption of constitutionality and that legislation may concern a single person or entity, but explained that whether those propositions apply depends on the circumstances. They did not justify selecting private succession claimants for exclusion based on a non-judicial report. The State’s legislative power is subject to fundamental rights.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_law and law_targets_specific_succession_claimants and law_dismisses_their_claims and law_prevents_court_adjudication and law_purpose_is_ending_private_dispute and law_relies_on_nonjudicial_adverse_report and no_exceptional_basis_for_differential_treatment

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_law: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law in a court proceeding.
predicates.law_targets_specific_succession_claimant: The law selects particular people asserting rights to inherit an estate for different treatment from other claimants.
predicates.law_dismisses_their_claims: The law itself rejects the selected claimants’ asserted inheritance claims.
predicates.law_prevents_court_adjudication: The law prevents the selected claimants from establishing their asserted rights through ordinary court proceedings.
predicates.law_purpose_is_ending_private_dispute: The law’s purpose is to end a dispute between private claimants rather than to secure a public advantage.
predicates.law_relies_on_nonjudicial_adverse_report: The law’s treatment of the selected claimants rests on an adverse finding by an authority that did not decide the dispute as a court.
predicates.no_exceptional_basis_for_differential_tr: The dispute’s circumstances do not provide a rational and exceptional basis for treating the selected claimants differently from others in the same position.

issues.definition: When a challenged law singles out succession claimants, rejects their claims and bars court adjudication to end a private dispute on the basis of a non-judicial adverse report, without an exceptional rational basis for the distinction, the law is invalid for unequal treatment.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant need not already possess a decree or established property interest for discriminatory legislation that deprives the claimant of an asserted inheritance right to engage the equal-protection guarantee.
material_facts: The claimants sought to assert inheritance rights under the general law governing their community.
Whether the claimants had already obtained a final and enforceable decree remained pending before a lower court.
The legislation itself dismissed their claims, and the Court treated their asserted claim to the estate as a valuable right.
issues.conclusion: The applicability of Article 14 did not depend on whether the claimants had already acquired property in the form of a decree; their asserted inheritance claim was itself a valuable right whose discriminatory deprivation could engage Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 applies where discriminatory legislation deprives a person of a valuable right asserted under the general law. The existence of a prior decree establishing that right is not a prerequisite. The Court left open whether a final and effective decree had in fact been made.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_law: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law in a court proceeding.
predicates.claimant_asserts_inheritance_under_gener: A person claims an entitlement to inherit under the law generally governing the relevant community.
predicates.law_discriminates_against_claimant_by_de: The challenged law treats the claimant unequally by taking away or rejecting the asserted inheritance claim.
predicates.existence_of_prior_decree_is_unresolved: Whether a court has already made a final decree establishing the asserted right remains undecided.

issues.definition: If a claimant asserts an inheritance right under general law and discriminatory legislation deprives the claimant of that asserted right, equal-protection review does not depend on whether a prior decree exists.
